offending.as_cited: Harris v. Illinois Human Rights Comm'n, 2022 IL App (1st) 210454
offending.cited_case_name: Harris v. Illinois Human Rights Comm'n
offending.court_quote: Petitioner's briefs also contain false case citations. One such case, “Harris v. Illinois Human Rights Comm'n, 2022 IL App (1st) 210454,” does not exist at all. The citation 2022 IL App (1st) 210454-U leads to a criminal case named People v. Riley-Palmer.
offending.what_actually_exists: The neutral citation 2022 IL App (1st) 210454-U exists but belongs to People v. Riley-Palmer, a criminal case unrelated to human rights law.

offending.quoted_text: definition of arbitrary and capricious action
offending.court_quote: In addition, petitioner quotes language that does not appear in the cases cited. For example, Gusciara v. Lustig, 346 Ill. App. 3d 1012 (2004), does not include a “definition of arbitrary and capricious action.”
offending.what_actually_exists: Gusciara v. Lustig, 346 Ill. App. 3d 1012 (2004) is a real Illinois Appellate Court decision but contains no definition of arbitrary and capricious action.

offending.as_cited: Village of Oak Lawn v. Illinois Human Rights Comm'n, 133 Ill. App. 3d 221 (1985)
offending.cited_case_name: Village of Oak Lawn v. Illinois Human Rights Comm'n
offending.quoted_text: evidence a reasonable mind might accept as sufficient to support a conclusion
offending.court_quote: Village of Oak Lawn v. Illinois Human Rights Comm'n, 133 Ill. App. 3d 221 (1985), does not define “substantial evidence” as “evidence a reasonable mind might accept as sufficient to support a conclusion.”
offending.what_actually_exists: Village of Oak Lawn v. Illinois Human Rights Comm'n, 133 Ill. App. 3d 221 (1985) is real but contains no such definition of substantial evidence.

offending.as_cited: Abrahamson v. Illinois Department of Professional Regulation, 153 Ill. 2d 76, 88 (1992)
offending.cited_case_name: Abrahamson v. Illinois Department of Professional Regulation
offending.court_quote: And Abrahamson v. Illinois Department of Professional Regulation, 153 Ill. 2d 76, 88 (1992), does not describe a “reasoned consideration” standard for agency decisions.
offending.what_actually_exists: Abrahamson, 153 Ill. 2d 76 (1992) is a real Illinois Supreme Court decision but describes no “reasoned consideration” standard.

offending.as_cited: Abrahamson v. Illinois Department of Professional Regulation, 153 Ill. 2d 76 (1992)
offending.cited_case_name: Abrahamson v. Illinois Department of Professional Regulation
offending.quoted_text: [w]hether an administrative agency correctly applied the law is subject to de novo review
offending.court_quote: Finally, petitioner cites cases that do not support the propositions of law for which petitioner cites them. For example, petitioner cites Abrahamson for the proposition that “[w]hether an administrative agency correctly applied the law is subject to de novo review.” But Abrahamson does not mention de novo review.
offending.what_actually_exists: Abrahamson is real but does not mention de novo review.

offending.as_cited: Hall v. Naper Gold Hospitality, LLC, 2012 IL App (2d) 111151, ¶ 7
offending.cited_case_name: Hall v. Naper Gold Hospitality, LLC
offending.quoted_text: Illinois reviewing courts routinely decline to strike briefs where the issues presented are sufficiently clear to permit meaningful review
offending.court_quote: Petitioner also cites Hall v. Naper Gold Hospitality, LLC, 2012 IL App (2d) 111151, ¶ 7, to claim that “Illinois reviewing courts routinely decline to strike briefs where the issues presented are sufficiently clear to permit meaningful review.” But paragraph 7 of Hall actually supports striking briefs as a sanction for noncompliance with Illinois Supreme Court rules. Id. ¶¶ 7, 15.
offending.what_actually_exists: Hall v. Naper Gold Hospitality, LLC, 2012 IL App (2d) 111151 is real; ¶¶ 7 and 15 support the opposite proposition — striking briefs as a sanction for rule noncompliance.

offending.as_cited: Whipple v. Department of Rehabilitation Services, 269 Ill. App. 3d 554 (1995)
offending.cited_case_name: Whipple v. Department of Rehabilitation Services
offending.quoted_text: [a]n appellate court's review of a Human Rights Commission order follows the same framework applicable under the Administrative Review Law
offending.court_quote: Petitioner cites Whipple v. Department of Rehabilitation Services, 269 Ill. App. 3d 554 (1995), for the proposition that “[a]n appellate court's review of a Human Rights Commission order follows the same framework applicable under the Administrative Review Law,” but Whipple says no such thing.
offending.what_actually_exists: Whipple v. Department of Rehabilitation Services, 269 Ill. App. 3d 554 (1995) is real but says no such thing.

offending.quoted_text: The Department shall conduct a full investigation of the allegations set forth in the charge and shall determine whether substantial evidence exists that a civil rights violation has been committed.
offending.court_quote: Instead, petitioner misquotes inapplicable statutes and fabricates statutory language. Petitioner's brief's “Statutes Involved” section claims that section 7A-102(D)(2) of the Act provides: “The Department shall conduct a full investigation of the allegations set forth in the charge and shall determine whether substantial evidence exists that a civil rights violation has been committed.”
offending.what_actually_exists: Section 7A-102(D)(2) actually provides: “Upon review of the [Department's] report, the Director shall determine whether there is substantial evidence that the alleged civil rights violation has been committed. …” There is no “full investigation” requirement; the court held the requirement was “a product of AI-hallucinated language” (¶ 44).

offending.quoted_text: Any complainant or respondent aggrieved by a final order of the Commission may obtain judicial review thereof in the Appellate Court for the district in which the alleged civil rights violation occurred, in accordance with the provisions of the Administrative Review Law, as modified by Supreme Court Rule 335.
offending.court_quote: Respondents identified the two false quotations discussed above, but petitioner's brief also claims that section 8-111(B)(1) of the Act provides: “Any complainant or respondent aggrieved by a final order of the Commission may obtain judicial review thereof in the Appellate Court for the district in which the alleged civil rights violation occurred, in accordance with the provisions of the Administrative Review Law, as modified by Supreme Court Rule 335.”
offending.what_actually_exists: Section 8-111(B)(1) actually provides: “Any complainant or respondent may apply for and obtain judicial review of a final order of the Commission entered under this Act by filing a petition for review in the Appellate Court within 35 days from the date that a copy of the decision sought to be reviewed was served upon the party affected by the decision. …”

offending.quoted_text: if the Director determines there is a lack of substantial evidence, the Department will dismiss the charge
offending.filing: Attorney Cole's response to the show-cause order, footnote 1
offending.court_quote: Frustratingly, attorney Cole's response itself contains misstatements of law. Footnote 1 claims that “under 775 ILCS 5/7A-102(D)(2)(a), if the Director determines there is a lack of substantial evidence, the Department will dismiss the charge.” The applicable version of section 7A-102 has no subsection (D)(2)(a). … Moreover, the “substantial evidence” language attorney Cole purports to quote appears in subsection (D)(3), not (D)(2).
offending.what_actually_exists: There is no subsection (D)(2)(a) in the applicable version of § 7A-102; the legislature removed it effective 1 January 2008 (Pub. Act 95-243). The quoted “substantial evidence” language appears in subsection (D)(3).

controls.as_cited: Jabbari v. Human Rights Comm'n, 173 Ill. App. 3d 227, 232 (1988)
